# The Department of Small Repairs

When the town council announced that it was closing the Department of Small Repairs, most people assumed it was a joke.

The department occupied a narrow room behind the post office. Its window displayed a clock that had stopped at twenty past three, a blue ceramic bird with one wing glued back on, and a handwritten sign that said:

**IF IT CAN BE MENDED, WE WILL TRY.  
IF IT CANNOT, WE WILL TELL YOU GENTLY.**

The clock had not been left there as an advertisement. It belonged to the department’s only employee, a woman named Mara, who had been meaning to fix it for eleven years.

For nearly four decades, residents had brought her objects that were broken but not, in their owners’ judgment, finished: umbrellas that would not open, lamps that would not light, drawers that refused to remain closed. Mara repaired these things when she could. When she could not, she often found them a second life. A teapot with a cracked spout became a planter. A wooden ladder with one missing rung became a shelf for shoes.

The department charged according to an old schedule taped beside the door. Most prices were absurdly low. A loose button cost twenty cents. A bicycle bell cost fifty. Anything requiring more than an hour was listed as “to be discussed,” which usually meant Mara would accept a jar of jam, a ride to the hardware store, or nothing at all.

The council called it an inefficient use of public funds. A neighboring town, the mayor pointed out, had replaced its repair service with a website listing private contractors.

“How many people actually use it?” he asked at the meeting.

The finance clerk checked her notes. “Last year, four hundred and twelve visits.”

“Out of a population of eight thousand.”

“Yes.”

The mayor nodded, as if the number settled the matter. The room was nearly empty. Nobody spoke against the proposal, and the department was scheduled to close at the end of September.

Mara learned about the decision from a printed notice slipped beneath her door.

She read it twice, put it under the blue bird, and went back to work on a toaster.

---

The first person she told was a boy named Ivo, who came in every Thursday after school with his grandmother’s shopping cart. The cart had a squeaking wheel that Mara had repaired six times. Each repair lasted a few weeks before the squeak returned.

“You’re closing?” Ivo asked.

“Apparently.”

“Where will the things go?”

“Some will go home. The tools belong to the council, so I suppose they’ll go into storage.”

“I meant the things people bring.”

Mara considered this. “I suppose people will have to find someone else.”

Ivo looked around the room. On the counter sat a radio with its back removed, a purse missing a clasp, and a green watering can with a hole near the handle. Above them hung a photograph of the town’s old railway station, which had been demolished before he was born.

“Who else can fix all this?”

“There are people who know more than I do about most things in here,” Mara said. “They’re just harder to find.”

She turned the cart upside down and examined its wheel. Ivo had wrapped the axle in a strip of blue cloth, which was already fraying.

“Was this your repair?”

He nodded.

“It was worth trying.”

“It didn’t work.”

“It worked for a while.”

“That’s not the same.”

“No,” Mara said. “But it’s not nothing.”

She removed the cloth, cleaned the axle, and fitted a small washer from a tin beneath the counter. When she set the cart upright, it rolled silently across the floor.

Ivo pushed it back and forth. “How long will it last?”

“I don’t know. If it starts squeaking again, bring it before September.”

He left with the cart and returned ten minutes later without it.

“Can I help you stay open?” he asked.

Mara was searching for a screw she had dropped. “You can help me find that first.”

They found it beneath the radiator.

---

Ivo’s grandmother, Mrs. Bell, said the council had made up its mind and that petitions rarely changed anything. Nevertheless, she signed the petition Ivo wrote, then took it to the bakery.

The baker signed because Mara had repaired the latch on his back gate. A woman buying rye bread signed because Mara had shortened the strap on her father’s medical bag after he died, so she could carry it herself. The baker’s apprentice signed because he liked Ivo, although he had never visited the department.

By the end of the week, the petition had thirty-seven names.

Ivo brought it to Mara, expecting approval. She read every name, including one that had been crossed out and rewritten because its owner had misspelled his own surname.

“Thank you,” she said.

“Is thirty-seven enough?”

“I doubt it.”

“How many do we need?”

“I don’t know that either.”

She pinned the petition beside the price list. The next morning, a man collecting his repaired lamp added his name. Later, a woman came in specifically to sign and stayed for twenty minutes, telling Mara about a music box she had owned as a child.

Mara listened, though she was unsure what the woman wanted from her. At last the woman took the music box from her handbag. It was small and pale green, painted with roses.

“It stopped years ago,” she said. “I thought perhaps you could look.”

The spring was broken. Mara did not have a replacement, and the mechanism was delicate enough that she was reluctant to improvise. She told the woman she would ask around.

The woman seemed disappointed, but she signed the petition before leaving.

That evening Mara telephoned a retired watchmaker in the next town. He knew where she might order a spring, though he warned her it could take months to arrive.

“Months might be too long,” Mara said.

“Then give them my number,” he replied.

---

As news of the closure spread, the department became busier than it had been in years. Some people came because they wanted a repair before the service disappeared. Others came because they wanted to see the place they had heard about and found something to bring with them.

A man arrived with a wooden duck whose head had fallen off. A schoolteacher brought a globe that had stopped turning on its stand. A teenager brought a cassette player she had bought at a market, along with a tape labeled **SUMMER 1998**.

“My mother made it,” she explained. “She says she doesn’t remember what’s on it.”

The cassette player needed a new belt. Mara ordered one and, while they waited, lent the girl an old player from the cupboard.

The girl returned the next day with a list of songs she and her mother had identified. There were two they could not name. At the end of the tape, after a long silence, they had heard a dog barking and someone laughing very close to the microphone.

“Was it your mother?” Mara asked.

“I think so. She thinks it was my aunt.”

The girl played that part three times, hoping Mara could settle the question. Mara could not, but she enjoyed listening.

Not every repair went well. Mara broke the brittle plastic catch on a lunch box while trying to replace its hinge. She apologized to the owner, a little girl who had waited beside the counter through the entire procedure.

The girl examined the damage and began to cry. Her father told her he would buy her a new lunch box, which made her cry harder.

Mara offered to make a leather strap that would hold the lid shut. The girl did not answer. She took the lunch box home, and for two days Mara assumed she would not see it again.

On the third day, the girl returned with her father and asked whether the strap could be red.

---

At the council’s next meeting, Ivo stood up during the public comment period and presented the petition. It had two hundred and six signatures.

The mayor thanked him and said that the council appreciated the community’s affection for the department. He also explained that the town faced rising costs: the school roof needed work, the water pipes beneath Alder Street had to be replaced, and the fire station’s engine was due for an expensive inspection.

“We have to make choices,” he said.

Ivo had prepared a speech, but it depended on the mayor being unreasonable. Faced with the list of repairs, he lost his place.

“Couldn’t you close something else?” he asked.

“Possibly,” said the mayor. “What would you suggest?”

Ivo looked at the council members. Behind them hung framed photographs of previous mayors, all wearing the same serious expression.

“I don’t know,” he admitted.

Afterward, the finance clerk found him in the corridor and showed him the budget. The department’s largest expense was Mara’s salary. There was also rent for the room, electricity, insurance, and a small allowance for supplies.

“Could volunteers run it?” Ivo asked.

“They might,” the clerk said. “But someone would have to organize them, and the council would still need to decide who was responsible if something went wrong.”

She did not say it to discourage him. She wrote the questions on the back of an agenda and gave it to him to take home.

That evening, Ivo and his grandmother spread the budget across their kitchen table. Mrs. Bell knew how to keep accounts; she had done them for her brother’s plumbing business for twenty years. She also knew people who might be willing to volunteer.

“First,” she said, “we need to ask Mara whether she wants to keep doing this.”

“She does,” Ivo said.

“Let’s ask her anyway.”

---

Mara wanted the department to stay open, but she was less certain about her own future. She had been thinking about retirement for some time. Her hands ached in cold weather, and she had begun to turn away repairs involving very small screws.

“I thought I might leave next spring,” she told Mrs. Bell and Ivo. “I hadn’t told anyone yet.”

Ivo stared at her. “But then who would do it?”

“That’s what we need to find out.”

The three of them made a list of people with useful skills. Some were professionals who might donate an occasional hour. Others were hobbyists, retirees, or people who had once mentioned knowing how to sew, sharpen blades, or repair radios.

The baker’s apprentice knew how to mend bicycle tires. The retired watchmaker agreed to visit once a month, provided someone collected him from the bus station. The schoolteacher with the globe offered to keep records. A tailor named Arun said he could come on Wednesdays after closing his shop.

By the following week, they had twelve volunteers and a problem: only Mara had a key to the department, and the council had not agreed to let anyone else use it.

The finance clerk suggested they submit a proposal. Ivo imagined a single page with everyone’s names on it, but Mrs. Bell insisted on a proper budget, a schedule, and a plan for handling complaints.

“What sort of complaints?” Ivo asked.

“The lunch box, for one.”

“It got a strap.”

“After Mara broke it. Suppose the owner had wanted her to pay for a new one.”

Mara nodded. “That’s fair. We should explain the risks before we start.”

They spent three evenings writing the proposal. Ivo designed a sign-up sheet, then redesigned it after discovering that his first version had no space for telephone numbers. Mrs. Bell called the insurance company. Mara counted tools and made a list of those she owned personally.

When the document was finished, it was eleven pages long. Ivo thought it looked important enough to work.

---

The council considered the proposal in August. The volunteers offered to run the department three days a week. They requested use of the room and its existing equipment, along with enough funding to cover insurance, utilities, and basic supplies.

The mayor asked what would happen if the volunteers lost interest.

“We’ll review the arrangement after six months,” Mrs. Bell said. “If we can’t keep the hours we’ve promised, you can end it.”

A council member asked whether local repair businesses objected to a free public service. Arun, the tailor, attended the meeting to answer. He said the department had referred customers to him for years, especially when a garment needed more work than Mara could manage.

“I’m not worried about losing business,” he said. “I’m worried about people throwing away a good coat because the lining has come loose.”

Another council member questioned whether volunteers could safely repair electrical appliances. Mara agreed that they needed limits. They proposed inspecting lamps and radios but referring complicated electrical work to qualified technicians.

The discussion lasted an hour. Ivo counted each minute on the clock above the door. When the council finally voted, the proposal passed by four votes to three.

The department would remain open for a six-month trial.

Outside, Ivo expected Mara to cheer. Instead, she sat on a bench and took a long breath.

“Are you happy?” he asked.

“Yes,” she said. “I’m also thinking about everything we’ve promised to do by Monday.”

He sat beside her. After a moment, she smiled.

“You did well in there.”

“I only carried the papers.”

“You carried them to the right place.”

Mrs. Bell came out with the finance clerk, who had already begun discussing forms. The four of them walked back toward the post office together, talking about keys, storage, and where they might put a second worktable.

---

The trial began unevenly.

On the first Monday, three volunteers arrived at nine, but nobody had remembered to unlock the cupboard containing the extension cords. On Wednesday, Arun discovered that the sewing machine needed a part Mara had ordered in June and forgotten to collect. On Friday, a customer brought in a chair, and the volunteers spent fifteen minutes deciding whether furniture counted as a small repair.

“It depends on the chair,” Mara said when she arrived.

This chair needed two joints reglued. They took it.

The volunteers developed a system. Each object received a numbered tag and a short description of the problem. Owners signed a form acknowledging that repairs might fail. Anything valuable, dangerous, or beyond the volunteers’ abilities was referred elsewhere.

Some visitors disliked the forms. One man announced that he had never been asked to sign anything when Mara worked alone.

“That was probably my mistake,” Mara told him.

He signed.

The worktable filled quickly. There were coats with torn pockets, a chessboard missing two squares of veneer, a pair of binoculars with a loose eyepiece, and a toy train that moved only when pushed. The volunteers learned to leave notes for one another. At first the notes were cryptic:

**SPRING IN TIN. DO NOT LOSE.**

Later they became more useful:

**Music box: replacement spring ordered. Owner is Mrs. Denby. Please call when it arrives. Number in ledger.**

Ivo came after school to sort screws, greet customers, and sweep the floor. He also learned that sorting screws was harder than it sounded. A single jar could contain a dozen sizes that looked nearly identical until someone needed a particular one.

Mara showed him how to measure them and where to find the thread gauge. He made labels for the drawers, then corrected several after the watchmaker pointed out that he had mixed up millimeters and fractions of an inch.

---

In October, the replacement spring for Mrs. Denby’s music box arrived.

The watchmaker fitted it while Mara and Ivo watched. He worked slowly, using a magnifying lens and a pair of tweezers so fine that Ivo was afraid to breathe near them.

When the mechanism was assembled, the watchmaker wound the key. The box played a tune none of them recognized. It was slightly uneven, with one note that sounded softer than the others, but it played all the way through.

Mrs. Denby came the next morning. She opened the lid, listened, and began to hum. Then she stopped.

“I thought I remembered it,” she said.

She listened again. The tune did not change. Afterward, she told them that her sister used to keep the box on a shelf above their beds. Perhaps she had been remembering a song her sister sang, rather than the music in the box.

“Is your sister still nearby?” Mara asked.

“In Bristol.”

Mrs. Denby took out her telephone and called her. She held it close to the music box while the tune played. Her sister could hear it, though not very well, and promised to call back that evening from a quieter room.

Before leaving, Mrs. Denby placed the box carefully in her handbag. She offered to pay the watchmaker, who accepted the cost of the spring and a slice of the cake she had brought from home.

That afternoon, Ivo asked Mara whether she had known the repair would succeed.

“No.”

“Were you worried?”

“A little.”

“Because she’d waited so long?”

“And because the watchmaker might have broken something else while fitting the spring. Old mechanisms can be stubborn.”

“But it worked.”

“Yes,” Mara said. “We were lucky, and he was careful.”

---

By December, the department had enough volunteers to open an extra half day. The finance clerk visited to check the accounts and found them in good order, though Mrs. Bell had to explain three entries written in Ivo’s handwriting.

The council’s six-month review was still months away. Nobody knew whether the service would become permanent, but people had begun to speak about it without adding “if it stays open.”

Mara reduced her hours. On Tuesdays she went swimming. On some Thursdays she took a bus to the coast and walked along the promenade, stopping for soup at a café where the windows steamed in cold weather. She still came to the department twice a week, and sometimes on other days if someone called with a question.

One wet afternoon, she found Ivo standing beneath the blue bird with the stopped clock in his hands.

“Can I try?” he asked.

“You can, but it may not be a simple job.”

He opened the back under her supervision. Dust had collected around the mechanism, and one of the hands was loose. The clock also needed a new mainspring, which neither of them had in stock.

Ivo looked disappointed.

“We can order one,” Mara said.

They wrote down the measurements and put the clock back in the window. It remained at twenty past three through Christmas and most of January.

When the spring finally came, Ivo installed it with help from the watchmaker. He tightened the loose hand and polished the glass. Then he wound the clock and set it on the counter.

It ticked loudly enough for everyone in the room to hear.

For the rest of the day, people checked it against their telephones. At first it ran four minutes fast. Ivo adjusted the regulator, and by closing time it was only thirty seconds ahead.

He carried it to the window, where Mara helped him settle it between the blue bird and the sign. Outside, rainwater ran along the curb, carrying a paper receipt toward the drain. The baker passed with an umbrella, paused to wave, and continued up the street.

Inside, Ivo watched the clock for another minute. Its second hand moved steadily. He knew he would have to check it again tomorrow.

The watchmaker fitted it while Mara and Ivo watched. He worked slowly, using a magnifying lens and a pair of tweezers so fine that Ivo was afraid to breathe near them.

When the mechanism was assembled, the watchmaker wound the key. The box played a tune none of them recognized. It was slightly uneven, with one note that sounded softer than the others, but it played all the way through.

Mrs. Denby came the next morning. She opened the lid, listened, and began to hum. Then she stopped.

“I thought I remembered it,” she said.

She listened again. The tune did not change. Afterward, she told them that her sister used to keep the box on a shelf above their beds. Perhaps she had been remembering a song her sister sang, rather than the music in the box.

“Is your sister still nearby?” Mara asked.

“In Bristol.”

Mrs. Denby took out her telephone and called her. She held it close to the music box while the tune played. Her sister could hear it, though not very well, and promised to call back that evening from a quieter room.

Before leaving, Mrs. Denby placed the box carefully in her handbag. She offered to pay the watchmaker, who accepted the cost of the spring and a slice of the cake she had brought from home.

That afternoon, Ivo asked Mara whether she had known the repair would succeed.

“No.”

“Were you worried?”

“A little.”

“Because she’d waited so long?”

“And because the watchmaker might have broken something else while fitting the spring. Old mechanisms can be stubborn.”

“But it worked.”

“Yes,” Mara said. “We were lucky, and he was careful.”

---

By December, the department had enough volunteers to open an extra half day. The finance clerk visited to check the accounts and found them in good order, though Mrs. Bell had to explain three entries written in Ivo’s handwriting.

The council’s six-month review was still months away. Nobody knew whether the service would become permanent, but people had begun to speak about it without adding “if it stays open.”

Mara reduced her hours. On Tuesdays she went swimming. On some Thursdays she took a bus to the coast and walked along the promenade, stopping for soup at a café where the windows steamed in cold weather. She still came to the department twice a week, and sometimes on other days if someone called with a question.

One wet afternoon, she found Ivo standing beneath the blue bird with the stopped clock in his hands.

“Can I try?” he asked.

“You can, but it may not be a simple job.”

He opened the back under her supervision. Dust had collected around the mechanism, and one of the hands was loose. The clock also needed a new mainspring, which neither of them had in stock.

Ivo looked disappointed.

“We can order one,” Mara said.

They wrote down the measurements and put the clock back in the window. It remained at twenty past three through Christmas and most of January.

When the spring finally came, Ivo installed it with help from the watchmaker. He tightened the loose hand and polished the glass. Then he wound the clock and set it on the counter.

It ticked loudly enough for everyone in the room to hear.

For the rest of the day, people checked it against their telephones. At first it ran four minutes fast. Ivo adjusted the regulator, and by closing time it was only thirty seconds ahead.

He carried it to the window, where Mara helped him settle it between the blue bird and the sign. Outside, rainwater ran along the curb, carrying a paper receipt toward the drain. The baker passed with an umbrella, paused to wave, and continued up the street.

Inside, Ivo watched the clock for another minute. Its second hand moved steadily. He knew he would have to check it again tomorrow.
